note.text: Use an invented basket or teacher-supplied observations; no shopping or personal spending is required. Record item, unit, fixed quantity, base unit price and later unit price. Multiply quantity by unit price and add item costs in each period. Hold composition and quality constant for this model. A small classroom basket describes itself; it is not automatically representative of Cameroon’s national price level. Mark any missing quotation rather than inventing a price.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to record comparable quantities and costs and explain what a small basket can establish. Builds on: internal purchasing power and price indices. Leads to: inflation measurement and careful comparisons.

sections.heading: Understand the economics
sections.text: Use an invented basket or teacher-supplied observations; no shopping or personal spending is required. Record item, unit, fixed quantity, base unit price and later unit price. Multiply quantity by unit price and add item costs in each period. Hold composition and quality constant for this model. A small classroom basket describes itself; it is not automatically representative of Cameroon’s national price level. Mark any missing quotation rather than inventing a price.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: Original basket: {2} notebooks at {200} then {250} CFA francs each; {1} folder at {600} then {650}. Base cost is {2*200+600}; later cost is {2*250+650}. Price index is {100*(2*250+650)/(2*200+600)}. The comparison preserves quantities, units and quality. It does not measure the experience of every household.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Prepare the item record, calculate both totals and label the base. Check missing observations and comparable units. Explain the difference between a particular basket’s movement and a representative price index. A different basket needs its own weights and evidence.
